name: Obispeño
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

tone_statements.citation: Klar, Kathryn A. 1970. Topics in Obispeno Chumash: Part I. Class paper, Linguistics 195 (Fall 1970, Mary R. Haas), University of California, Berkeley. 16 pp. Item Haas.068.027, Miscellaneous papers from the Survey of California and Other Indian Languages, California Language Archive.
tone_statements.quote: A last problem was that of grave and acute marks which appear over many of the vowels. As with many of the diacritics Mr. Harrington uses, these do not seem distinctive. Admittedly, I know too little about them to know for sure what they represent, but the fact that their use is not consistent even in different instances of they [sic] same utterance leads me to believe that ignoring for the sake of clarity (for the time being, at least) is the most practical option.
tone_statements.locator: Orthography section = typescript p. 6 (the following page is numbered 7), last paragraph before 'Other orthographic changes', with footnote 5 on the same page (pónó’/pono’ 'tree' or 'pole'.. témè/teme 'squirrel', all of which appear in Mr. Harrington's data.'); phoneme chart 'The Sound System' = typescript p. 7 (vowels i e a ə o u; consonants only; no suprasegmental row).
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)

sources.citation: Klar, Kathryn A. 1992. John P. Harrington's phonetic representations of Obispeño Chumash palatal consonants. In James E. sources.note: Nothing on stress; discusses Harrington's two 'long s' graphs = č vs. palatalized t^y, evidence for two Obispeño dialects in Rosario Cooper's speech, and mentions an unpublished 'brief grammatical sketch of Obispeño' in Harrington's hand at the NAA.

sources.citation: Klar, Kathryn A. 1977. Topics in Historical Chumash Grammar. Ph.D. dissertation, University of California, Berkeley. 194 pp. (eScholarship item 31t2k96m).
sources.note: Nothing. Chapter 'Correspondences and Reconstructions I: The Proto-Chumash Phonological Inventory' (diss. pp.10-32 = pp.13-35) gives the Obispeño consonant and vowel inventory (pp.12-13), aspiration/gemination rules, the Obispeño t^y/q split and vowel ablaut; full-document scanned has zero hits for stress/accent/penult/syllable and the cited Obispeño forms carry no stress marks.

sources.citation: Heizer, Robert F. (ed.) 1955. California Indian linguistic records: The Mission Indian vocabularies of H. W. Henshaw. Anthropological Records 15(2):85-202.
sources.note: No rule; the Phonetic Key states 'The accented syllable of every word marked by an acute accent', so Henshaw's 1884 San Luis Obispo vocabulary (MS 852a, speaker Alikano) is accent-marked raw data from which stress position could be tallied.

sources.citation: Harrington, John P. n.d. [c.1916]. Brief grammatical sketch of Obispeño (fair copy in Harrington's hand) and Obispeño field notes/slipfiles from Rosario Cooper, 1912-1916. Papers of J. P. Harrington, National Anthropological Archives, Smithsonian (microfilm Vol. 3, Southern California/Basin, Obispeño reels; digitized at collections.si.edu / sova.si.edu).
sources.note: The only first-hand description by the sole fieldworker; Klar 1992 confirms a grammatical sketch exists; Harrington routinely marked stress, so either the sketch states a rule or the slips allow one to be tallied.
